benchmarks.summary: Parse one initialize request from JSON bytes.
benchmarks.what: The cost of parse_message on one initialize request: version check, key classification, and serde into a Request.
benchmarks.why: Every inbound MCP message pays this before a method runs. If this grows, the server is spending time on the envelope.
benchmarks.timing: one_initialize_bytes() runs before the bench and builds one JSON buffer. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: parse_message on that buffer, then black_box of the Message. Building the request and calling serde_json::to_vec for the fixture are excluded.
benchmarks.inputs: One initialize request. id is the number 1. protocolVersion is 2025-06-18. capabilities is {}. clientInfo is name bench, version 0.1.0. The same bytes are reused for every sample.
benchmarks.fake: Nothing is mocked. There is no socket, no clock sleep, and no rmcp session. The bytes are an in-memory Vec.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. One message should stay well under a millisecond. A jump means the message type or the JSON layer got heavier.

benchmarks.summary: Parse 1,000 initialize requests from JSON bytes.
benchmarks.what: The cost of calling parse_message once per buffer, 1,000 times, and counting the results.
benchmarks.why: A busy stdio server reads many messages. This is the parse cost of a batch with no transport between them.
benchmarks.timing: thousand_initialize_bytes() runs before the bench and builds 1,000 separate Vec<u8> values. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: a for loop over those buffers, parse_message, black_box of each Message, and a count. Fixture construction is excluded. The loop and the 1,000 parses are included.
benchmarks.inputs: 1,000 initialize requests. ids are the integers 0 through 999. Every other field matches parse_1_message. Each message is its own buffer.
benchmarks.fake: Nothing is mocked. The 1,000 buffers are already in memory. No framing, no stdin, no batch JSON array.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. This should stay well under 50 ms. It is about 1,000 times one parse, plus the loop, not 1,000 network round trips.

benchmarks.summary: Serialize one initialize request to JSON bytes.
benchmarks.what: The cost of serde_json::to_vec on one Message::Request.
benchmarks.why: Every outbound initialize or ping pays this on the way out.
benchmarks.timing: The Request is built before the bench and wrapped in Message::Request once. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: serde_json::to_vec of that message, then black_box of the bytes. Struct construction is excluded.
benchmarks.inputs: One initialize request, id 1, the same fields as parse_1_message. One struct, reused for every sample.
benchmarks.fake: Nothing is mocked. No socket. The output buffer is allocated inside the sample, which is part of the cost of sending.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. One message should stay well under a millisecond.

benchmarks.summary: Serialize 1,000 initialize requests to JSON bytes.
benchmarks.what: The cost of serde_json::to_vec on 1,000 already-built Message values, summing the byte lengths.
benchmarks.why: Shows the emit cost of a thousand similar envelopes without parsing them first.
benchmarks.timing: thousand_messages() runs before the bench and builds 1,000 Message values. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: to_vec for each message, add bytes.len() to a total, black_box of the bytes and the total. Building the 1,000 structs is excluded. The allocations of the output buffers are included.
benchmarks.inputs: 1,000 initialize requests. ids are 0 through 999. Same fields as parse_1_message otherwise.
benchmarks.fake: Nothing is mocked. No socket and no batching into one JSON array. One object per message.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. This should stay well under 50 ms.

benchmarks.summary: Dispatch one already-parsed initialize request.
benchmarks.what: The cost of dispatch on a Message::Request: match the method, parse InitializeParams, build InitializeResult, and wrap a success Response.
benchmarks.why: This is the work after the bytes are already a Message. It is the floor under an initialize that does not touch a transport.
benchmarks.timing: The Message is built before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: dispatch of that message, then black_box of the Option<Response>. Parsing bytes is excluded. serde_json::to_value of the result struct is included, because dispatch does that before it returns.
benchmarks.inputs: One initialize request, id 1, protocolVersion 2025-06-18, empty capabilities, clientInfo name bench version 0.1.0. The server answer is protocolVersion 2025-06-18, empty capabilities, serverInfo name fastmcp-rs version 0.1.0, no instructions.
benchmarks.fake: The server name and version are constants. Capabilities are an empty JSON object. There is no session, no middleware, and no clock.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. One initialize dispatch should stay well under a millisecond. Milliseconds would mean the handler started doing real work this chapter does not do.

benchmarks.summary: Choose one protocol version.
benchmarks.what: The cost of choose_version for a supported handshake version: a contains check on a five-element const slice and a clone of the version.
benchmarks.why: Every initialize pays this before the session continues. It should stay noise next to parsing a message.
benchmarks.timing: The requested version is built before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: choose_version against SUPPORTED_VERSIONS, then black_box of the chosen version. Building the const slice is excluded.
benchmarks.inputs: Requested version 2025-06-18. The supported slice is the five dates from 2024-11-05 through 2026-07-28.
benchmarks.fake: Nothing is mocked. There is no socket, no rmcp serve loop, and no client.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. One choice should stay well under a microsecond. About 10 ns locally.

benchmarks.summary: Choose a protocol version 1,000 times.
benchmarks.what: The cost of 1,000 choose_version calls. Every fifth request is 2026-07-28, which falls back to 2025-11-25. The rest echo 2025-06-18.
benchmarks.why: A process that accepts many clients repeats this choice. The fallback path has to stay cheap too.
benchmarks.timing: The Vec of 1,000 versions is built before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: choose_version for each entry and black_box of the last result. Building the Vec is excluded.
benchmarks.inputs: 1,000 versions. Indexes divisible by 5 are 2026-07-28. The others are 2025-06-18. The same Vec is reused for every sample.
benchmarks.fake: Nothing is mocked. No session and no socket.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. A thousand choices should stay well under a millisecond. About 12 µs locally.

benchmarks.summary: Initialize and list tools on an in-memory stdio transport.
benchmarks.what: The cost of one duplex pipe, rmcp serve on one end, a client initialize for 2025-06-18, one tools/list, and cancel.
benchmarks.why: This is the first time the book times a session. It shows the floor under handshake plus tools/list when the bytes never leave the process.
benchmarks.timing: The multi-thread Tokio runtime is built before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: tokio::io::duplex, spawn the server, client serve (which runs initialize), list_tools, cancel, and black_box of the tool count. Runtime construction is excluded. Process spawn is not part of the sample.
benchmarks.inputs: Server name fastmcp-rs, version 0.1.0. Client protocol version 2025-06-18. The server answers with that version and one status tool.
benchmarks.fake: The pipe is tokio::io::duplex, not the terminal's stdin and stdout. It is the same AsyncRead and AsyncWrite transport rmcp::transport::stdio uses. No child process.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. One session should stay well under 5 ms. About 114 µs locally. A jump into milliseconds of process startup would mean the bench started spawning a binary.

benchmarks.chapter: Chapter 3 The FastMcp builder and tools
benchmarks.summary: Look up one tool in a registry of 1,000.
benchmarks.what: The cost of HashMap::contains_key for tool-500 on a server that holds tool-0 through tool-999.
benchmarks.why: tools/call starts with a name lookup. The lookup should stay noise next to deserializing the arguments.
benchmarks.timing: thousand() runs before the bench and registers 1,000 tools. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: has_tool on the name tool-500, then black_box of the bool. Building the server and the closures is excluded.
benchmarks.inputs: 1,000 tools named tool-0 through tool-999. Each closure takes Echo { n: i64 } and returns n. The looked-up name is tool-500.
benchmarks.fake: Nothing is mocked. There is no JSON parse in this sample, no socket, and no tools/call. status is not one of the 1,000 keys.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. One lookup should stay well under a microsecond. About 13 ns locally.

benchmarks.chapter: Chapter 3 The FastMcp builder and tools
benchmarks.summary: Deserialize and call 1,000 registered tools.
benchmarks.what: The cost of dispatch_tool for every tool from tool-0 through tool-999: map lookup, clone of the argument JSON, serde into Echo, and the closure.
benchmarks.why: This is the registry's work for a batch of calls with no transport between them.
benchmarks.timing: The server, the Vec of 1,000 names, and the argument JSON are built before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: dispatch_tool for each name with a clone of {"n": 1}, then black_box of the last Result. Registration is excluded. The clone, the deserialize, and the closure are included.
benchmarks.inputs: 1,000 tools. Each call receives the object {"n": 1}. The closure returns the number 1.
benchmarks.fake: No socket and no rmcp session. status is not called. The argument object is real JSON, cloned once per call.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. A thousand calls should stay well under a millisecond. About 60 µs locally.

benchmarks.summary: Generate one JSON Schema from a struct.
benchmarks.what: The cost of json_schema_of for Greet: draft 2020-12 generation, serde_json::to_value, and removal of the top-level title and description.
benchmarks.why: Every .tool() registration pays this once for the argument type and once for the return type. It should stay far below a tool call.
benchmarks.timing: Nothing is built before the bench except the type itself, which is compiled in. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: json_schema_of::<Greet>() and black_box of the Arc. There is no cache and no FastMcp.
benchmarks.inputs: Greet has name: String and title: Option<String>. The schema's required array contains name and omits title.
benchmarks.fake: Nothing is mocked. No socket, no tools/list, and no TypeId cache. rmcp caches this kind of schema; this function does not.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. One schema should stay well under 100 microseconds. About 1.6 µs locally.

benchmarks.summary: Generate the same JSON Schema 1,000 times.
benchmarks.what: The cost of 1,000 uncached json_schema_of::<Greet>() calls.
benchmarks.why: Shows the generator's cost across a batch of registrations that do not share a cache. A cache would hide the work after the first call.
benchmarks.timing: The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: a loop of 1,000 generations and black_box of the last Arc. No server is built. No schema is reused across iterations of the loop.
benchmarks.inputs: The same Greet struct on every iteration. name is String. title is Option<String>.
benchmarks.fake: No socket and no cache. The repetition is the point: each call builds a new document.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. A thousand uncached generations should stay well under 50 ms. About 1.9 ms locally.

benchmarks.summary: Register one tool through the struct the macro emitted.
benchmarks.what: The cost of FastMcp::new plus tool_decl::<AddTool>, including the schema generation inside tool.
benchmarks.why: The proc macro already ran at compile time. This is the runtime cost that is still left: building the server and the schema.
benchmarks.timing: The AddTool type is compiled in. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: FastMcp::new and tool_decl, then black_box of the server. No dispatch_tool. The macro expansion is excluded.
benchmarks.inputs: add(left: i64, right: i64) -> Sum, description "add two integers".
benchmarks.fake: No socket. The schema is generated, not loaded from a file.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. One registration should stay well under 100 microseconds. About 3.2 µs locally.

benchmarks.summary: Call the function the macro left in place, 1,000 times.
benchmarks.what: The cost of add(n, 1) in a loop of 1,000, summing the totals.
benchmarks.why: Shows the function after expansion. Registration and schema generation are a different cost.
benchmarks.timing: The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: the loop, the calls, and black_box of the total. No FastMcp is constructed.
benchmarks.inputs: n runs from 0 through 999. The second argument is 1.
benchmarks.fake: No server, no JSON, no socket.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. A thousand calls should stay well under 10 microseconds. About 263 ns locally.

benchmarks.summary: Read one static resource from a map of 10,000.
benchmarks.what: The cost of FastMcp::read on a URI that is present in the static HashMap.
benchmarks.why: An exact URI should not scan templates. This is the cost of the hit.
benchmarks.timing: ten_thousand_static() runs before the bench and registers file://doc-0 through file://doc-9999. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: one read of file://doc-5000, then black_box. Building the map is excluded.
benchmarks.inputs: 10,000 static resources, MIME text/plain, body "body". The looked-up URI is file://doc-5000.
benchmarks.fake: No socket. The body is a String already stored on the server. The read clones it.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. One lookup should stay well under 1 microsecond. About 39 ns locally.

benchmarks.summary: Scan 10,000 URI templates and render the last match.
benchmarks.what: The cost of FastMcp::read when the URI misses the static map and matches the last registered template.
benchmarks.why: Templates are a list. The worst case walks every pattern, copies the capture, and runs the closure.
benchmarks.timing: ten_thousand_templates() runs before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: one read of res://item-9999/readme, then black_box. Registration is excluded. The scan, the String copy, and the closure are included.
benchmarks.inputs: Patterns res://item-0/{name} through res://item-9999/{name}. The URI matches item-9999. The closure returns "found".
benchmarks.fake: No socket and no filesystem. The closure ignores the capture and returns a constant.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. A full scan of 10,000 templates should stay well under 1 millisecond. About 264 µs locally.

benchmarks.summary: Render one prompt from an argument map.
benchmarks.what: The cost of FastMcp::render_prompt for greet with name Ada.
benchmarks.why: prompts/get pays this after the argument map is built. It is the template, not the session.
benchmarks.timing: greet() runs before the bench and builds the server and the HashMap. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: render_prompt, then black_box. Registration is excluded.
benchmarks.inputs: Prompt greet, required argument name, value Ada. The closure formats Hello, {name}.
benchmarks.fake: No socket. The argument map is already owned.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. One render should stay well under 1 microsecond. About 62 ns locally.

benchmarks.summary: Take one page from the middle of 10,000 items.
benchmarks.what: The cost of paginate_sequence: decode a cursor, skip to offset 5000, take 50 items, clone them, encode the next cursor.
benchmarks.why: Every list_* page pays this. The bench is the pager, so a slow number is the slice and the cursor, not the transport.
benchmarks.timing: The 10,000 strings and the starting cursor are built before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: paginate_sequence, then black_box. Fixture construction is excluded.
benchmarks.inputs: Items item-0 through item-9999. Page size 50. Cursor offset 5000.
benchmarks.fake: No socket and no rmcp session. The items are Strings in a Vec.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. One page should stay well under 50 microseconds. About 2.5 µs locally.

benchmarks.summary: Dispatch one successful tool 1,000 times.
benchmarks.what: The cost of 1,000 dispatch_tool calls that deserialize Add, run the closure, and serialize Sum.
benchmarks.why: The happy path is the baseline the error path is compared with.
benchmarks.timing: The server and the argument JSON are built before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: a loop of 1,000 dispatch_tool calls, each cloning the JSON, then black_box of the last result.
benchmarks.inputs: Tool add. Arguments left 2, right 3. 1,000 calls of the same name.
benchmarks.fake: No socket. The JSON is an in-memory Value.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. A thousand successes should stay well under 1 millisecond. About 128 µs locally.

benchmarks.summary: Look up a missing tool 1,000 times.
benchmarks.what: The cost of 1,000 dispatch_tool calls whose name is not in the map.
benchmarks.why: The error path should skip deserialization and the closure. This measures that miss.
benchmarks.timing: The server and the argument JSON are built before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: a loop of 1,000 dispatch_tool calls of the name missing, each cloning the JSON, then black_box of the last error.
benchmarks.inputs: A server with only add. The name missing. The same argument JSON as the happy path, cloned and then unused.
benchmarks.fake: No socket. The closure does not run.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better, and below the happy path. A thousand misses should stay well under 1 millisecond. About 64 µs locally.

benchmarks.summary: Record 1,000 progress notes in memory.
benchmarks.what: The cost of 1,000 Context::report_progress calls into a Mutex<Vec>, then a clear.
benchmarks.why: Progress in this chapter is a shared list. This is that list, without a notification on the wire.
benchmarks.timing: The Context is built before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: the loop of 1,000 pushes, clear, and black_box of the context. Building the Arc is excluded.
benchmarks.inputs: progress is 0 through 999. total is Some(1000). message is None.
benchmarks.fake: No socket and no notifications/progress. The note is a struct.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. A thousand notes should stay well under 100 microseconds. About 14 µs locally.

benchmarks.summary: Extract Dep<Db> 1,000 times.
benchmarks.what: The cost of 1,000 FromContext lookups: TypeId, downcast, clone, and bias + n.
benchmarks.why: This is the injection overhead with no JSON and no socket, so it can be set next to a hand-passed Arc.
benchmarks.timing: The InjectCtx is built before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: the loop, from_context, the addition, and black_box of the total.
benchmarks.inputs: Db { bias: 1 }. n from 0 through 999.
benchmarks.fake: No socket and no dispatch_tool.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. A thousand extractions should stay well under 100 microseconds. About 12 µs locally.

benchmarks.summary: Clone an Arc<Db> by hand, 1,000 times.
benchmarks.what: The cost of 1,000 Arc::clone calls plus bias + n, with no TypeId lookup.
benchmarks.why: The comparison for injection. The work after the value is in hand matches inject_1000.
benchmarks.timing: The Arc is built before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: the loop, Arc::clone, the addition, and black_box of the total.
benchmarks.inputs: The same Db { bias: 1 }, already inside an Arc.
benchmarks.fake: No socket and no map.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. A thousand clones should stay well under 100 microseconds. About 15 µs locally.

benchmarks.summary: Four threads read one RwLock.
benchmarks.what: The cost of spawning four threads, 1,000 read locks each, and joining them.
benchmarks.why: Shared state is a lock. This is that lock under four readers, with spawn included.
benchmarks.timing: The RwLock and the string ready are built before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: four thread::spawn calls, the reads, the joins, and black_box of the summed lengths.
benchmarks.inputs: Banner ready. Four threads. 1,000 reads each.
benchmarks.fake: No socket and no database. The string is already in the lock.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. The four threads should stay well under 2 milliseconds. About 244 µs locally.

benchmarks.summary: initialize, tools/list, and DELETE on loopback.
benchmarks.what: The cost of one handshake session: a TCP connect, an initialize POST, the SSE read, a tools/list POST, that read, and a DELETE.
benchmarks.why: This is the price of one client that opens a session and lists tools. Discover is a separate bench so the session cost stays visible.
benchmarks.timing: serve_http runs before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: post_mcp for initialize, post_mcp for tools/list, delete_mcp, and black_box of the list status.
benchmarks.inputs: protocolVersion 2025-06-18. Mcp-Method initialize, then tools/list with Mcp-Session-Id and MCP-Protocol-Version, then DELETE of that session.
benchmarks.fake: Loopback only. No TLS, no second machine, no event-store replay.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. One round trip should stay well under 2 milliseconds. About 295 µs locally.

benchmarks.summary: One initialize and a DELETE on loopback.
benchmarks.what: The cost of opening a handshake session and closing it, with no tools/list.
benchmarks.why: The comparison next to discover_once. Both are one request. This one also creates and deletes a session.
benchmarks.timing: serve_http runs before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: post_mcp for initialize, delete_mcp, and black_box of the status.
benchmarks.inputs: The same 2025-06-18 initialize body as http_roundtrip.
benchmarks.fake: Loopback only. No tools/list.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. One initialize should stay well under 1 millisecond. About 167 µs locally.

benchmarks.summary: One server/discover for 2026-07-28 on loopback.
benchmarks.what: The cost of a modern discover POST and the JSON read. No session is created.
benchmarks.why: This is the per-request cost of the 2026-07-28 era, set next to initialize_once.
benchmarks.timing: serve_http runs before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: post_mcp for server/discover and black_box of the status.
benchmarks.inputs: server/discover with MCP-Protocol-Version 2026-07-28, Mcp-Method server/discover, and _meta carrying the protocol version, client info, and client capabilities.
benchmarks.fake: Loopback only. No session id and no DELETE.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. One discover should stay well under 500 microseconds. About 91 µs locally.

benchmarks.summary: One in-process ask and submit.
benchmarks.what: The cost of building a Desk, spawning a task that submits yes, waiting on a oneshot, and joining.
benchmarks.why: This is one elicitation round with no socket, so the channel and the task switch are the number.
benchmarks.timing: Nothing is built before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: Desk::default, tokio::spawn of submit, ask, join, and black_box of the answer.
benchmarks.inputs: Message Ship it? and the value yes.
benchmarks.fake: The person is a spawned task. There is no tools/call and no schema check.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. One round should stay well under 100 microseconds. About 15 µs locally.

benchmarks.chapter: Chapter 14 The client and client groups
benchmarks.summary: One tools/list on a connected memory client.
benchmarks.what: The cost of one tools/list over an in-memory duplex, including the reply and the name collection.
benchmarks.why: This is the price of asking one server what it serves, after the handshake is already done.
benchmarks.timing: connect_memory runs before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: tool_names and black_box of the Vec.
benchmarks.inputs: One server. The only tool is status.
benchmarks.fake: No socket, no process, no HTTP. The duplex is already connected.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. One list should stay well under 200 microseconds. About 36 µs locally.

benchmarks.chapter: Chapter 14 The client and client groups
benchmarks.summary: tools/list across eight memory servers on a JoinSet.
benchmarks.what: The cost of eight lists in parallel, prefixing each tool, checking for a name collision, and sorting.
benchmarks.why: A group pays for every member. This is that fan-out with the connects already finished.
benchmarks.timing: Eight connect_memory calls and ClientGroup::new run before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: list_tools and black_box of the name count.
benchmarks.inputs: Servers s0 through s7. Each advertises status. Public names are s0_status through s7_status.
benchmarks.fake: No process and no HTTP. The peers are already up.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. Eight lists should stay well under 500 microseconds. About 79 µs locally.

benchmarks.summary: Tool names from the in-process harness.
benchmarks.what: The cost of collecting registered tool names and placing status first.
benchmarks.why: A unit test that calls the server directly should stay in the nanoseconds.
benchmarks.timing: The Harness is built before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: tool_names and black_box of the Vec.
benchmarks.inputs: A server named widgets with no extra tools. The list is the one name status.
benchmarks.fake: No socket, no duplex, no process.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. One list should stay well under 1 microsecond. About 24 ns locally.

benchmarks.summary: tools/list on a connected memory client.
benchmarks.what: The cost of one tools/list over the duplex that stdio tests use.
benchmarks.why: The protocol path is the comparison for the in-process harness.
benchmarks.timing: connect_memory runs before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: tool_names and black_box of the Vec.
benchmarks.inputs: A server named widgets. The only tool is status.
benchmarks.fake: No child process. The duplex is already connected.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. One list should stay well under 200 microseconds. About 53 µs locally.

benchmarks.summary: A thousand echo calls with no hooks.
benchmarks.what: The cost of invoke when the hook list is empty: dispatch, schema check, and the closure.
benchmarks.why: This is the baseline the five-layer chain is compared with.
benchmarks.timing: The server and the argument JSON are built before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: 1,000 invoke calls and black_box of each value.
benchmarks.inputs: echo with text hi, repeated 1,000 times.
benchmarks.fake: No hooks and no socket.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. A thousand calls should stay well under 2 milliseconds. About 194 µs locally.

benchmarks.summary: A thousand echo calls through five hooks.
benchmarks.what: The cost of two logs, a timer, a token bucket, and a size limit around each of 1,000 calls.
benchmarks.why: Each layer adds work on the way in and on the way out. This is that overhead with the tool still running.
benchmarks.timing: The server, the five hooks, and the argument JSON are built before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside it: 1,000 invoke calls.
benchmarks.inputs: echo with text hi. The bucket holds 1e15 tokens. The limit is 1,000,000 bytes.
benchmarks.fake: The cache is not in this timer. No socket.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. A thousand calls should stay well under 2 milliseconds. About 557 µs locally.
